newsitem.title: ITALY: Philip Morris fumes over Italian tax laws.
newsitem.headline: Philip Morris fumes over Italian tax laws.

text.p: U.S. tobacco giant Philip Morris Cos Inc criticised Italy's costly tax system on Thursday and complained that it had been wrongly accused of cheating the Treasury out of a small fortune in unpaid dues.
Senior managers from the group told a parliamentary commission that Italy's complex fiscal laws were earning the country a bad name among other multinationals.
Magistrates in Naples accused the U.S. company last July of avoiding payment of taxes on some 10 trillion lire ($6.5 billion) of revenues since 1987.
"The idea that Philip Morris was involved in tax evasion is groundless," the firm said in a written document which was presented to the lower house of parliament's finance commission.
It added that the charges, which are still under investigation, had much wider ramifications.
"Such behaviour is worrying for all non-resident economic operators who by now see Italy as an unpredictable fiscal country...and therefore a fiscal risk," the statement said.
Commission members criticised Philip Morris for the attack.

"If they've got all their papers in order, then all that is needed is to clear the case up and not make statements about fiscal risk which seem to us a bit superficial," commission chairman Giorgio Benvenuto told reporters.

Philip Morris, which makes the Marlboro brand, controls about 50 percent of the Italian cigarette market with sales of some 10 trillion lire in 1995. Around 7.5 trillion lire of this was eaten up in taxes, a Philip Morris official said.
The bulk of its cigarettes sold in Italy are made under licence by the state tabacco department Monopoli, which forms part of the finance ministry.
Investigators believe Philip Morris used a front company called Intertaba to take care of its Italian interests, thereby avoiding full taxation on royalties it received from Monopoli.
But Philip Morris executives told the commission that it had paid all the royalties -- some in the United States and others in Switzerland.
"The U.S. wants their taxes just like the Italian finance ministry wants theirs. They have to decide things between themselves," said Andre Reiman, senior vice president for Philip Morris Europe.
"One thing is for sure, we don't want to pay things twice over. We paid where we had to," he added.
Philip Morris executives complained they had to pay twice as much tax in Italy as in other European countries with similar fiscal systems, like Portugal, Spain and Greece.
They warned that the tax regime was encouraging widespread smuggling. "The economic returns caused by excessive taxation have attracted major organised crime," the company said.
It also charged that Monopoli's production costs were four times those in Philip Morris's own factories in the Netherlands and Germany, and said that this gap had to be narrowed.

The U.S. firm's contracts with Monopoli expire at the end of January. Finance Minister Vincenzo Visco told the parliamentary commission last year that Italy could not afford to break the link, which provides about 1,200 jobs.
